paragraphs: Training can benefit from accounting for how the loss curves around the current parameters, but computing an exact natural-gradient update is impractical for large neural networks. This paper introduces Kronecker Factors for Convolution, or KFC, to make this kind of curvature-aware optimization tractable for convolutional networks.

KFC builds an approximation to the Fisher matrix using a structured probabilistic model of backpropagated derivatives. Each matrix block separates into a Kronecker product of smaller matrices, making inversion efficient. This structure retains useful curvature information while keeping updates comparably efficient to stochastic gradient descent. The authors also show that common changes in parameterization, including centering activations, leave the updates invariant.

In the reported experiments, KFC trained convolutional networks several times faster than carefully tuned stochastic gradient descent and required 10–20 times fewer iterations. These are experimental results, while the reduced iteration count also suggests potential value for distributed training. The contribution connects a computationally manageable matrix approximation with both practical training improvements and a useful invariance property.
icml-2016-a-kronecker-factored-approxima.tldr: KFC approximates convolutional-network curvature efficiently and substantially accelerated training in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies echo-state neural networks through a random matrix framework. Its starting point is a distinction between understanding performance qualitatively and describing it quantitatively. Earlier work on recurrent networks, particularly linear versions, had offered insights into how different configurations affect behavior. The authors seek a mathematical counterpart that makes those performance insights more precise.

The approach uses random matrix analysis as the organizing framework for studying echo-state networks. Its role is to connect network configurations with quantitative descriptions of performance. The emphasis is therefore on analysis: understanding what happens under different configurations and explaining the mechanisms responsible for the resulting behavior.

The paper addresses both training and testing, making the relationship between fitting a network and assessing its subsequent performance part of the same investigation. Its stated contribution is a deeper account of the mechanisms operating in both stages, alongside quantitative performance results. This matters because qualitative observations can identify trends, while a quantitative framework can describe those trends with greater precision.
icml-2016-a-random-matrix-approach-to-ec.tldr: A random matrix framework gives quantitative explanations of echo-state network performance during training and testing.

paragraphs: This paper presents an optimization algorithm for objectives that may be convex or nonconvex and whose gradients are estimated from mini-batches. At each iteration, it multiplies the stochastic gradient by a symmetric positive definite scaling matrix. Updating this matrix over time lets the algorithm change how it scales and combines gradient directions.

The central design choice is to avoid imposing overly restrictive rules on those matrix updates. Instead, the method draws on self-correcting properties of BFGS-type updates. The authors argue that these properties had been overlooked in other efforts to adapt quasi-Newton optimization to stochastic settings. They use them as the basis for a dynamically changing metric.

Experiments on a few machine learning problems found that both the main algorithm and a limited-memory version were stable and outperformed mini-batch stochastic gradient and other quasi-Newton methods. The results support the practical usefulness of the design on those problems. The contribution is an approach to stochastic curvature adaptation that makes self-correction central to its update strategy.
icml-2016-a-self-correcting-variable-met.tldr: A stochastic variable-metric optimizer uses BFGS self-correction and performed well on several machine learning problems.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether reconstructing input images can improve networks already trained for large-scale supervised classification. The authors add decoding pathways to existing networks, allowing intermediate representations to support image reconstruction. This provides an unsupervised objective alongside the supervised task, even in a setting with abundant labeled images.

First, they show that intermediate activations of pretrained classification networks retain almost all input-image information, apart from some local spatial detail. They then train the augmented architecture end to end with the reconstruction objective and observe improved supervised performance. Several autoencoder designs are compared, including a what-where architecture that uses pooling switches from the encoder.

Using the 16-layer VGGNet under the ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 protocol as the baseline, the methods produce a noticeable improvement in validation accuracy. The findings indicate that reconstruction can provide useful training guidance even for a strong supervised network. They also make architecture design part of the investigation, examining how different decoding arrangements support the combined learning approach.
icml-2016-augmenting-supervised-neural-n.tldr: Adding image-reconstruction objectives to large supervised networks improved classification accuracy in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper introduces three semi-parametric extensions of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis, a framework for modeling related views of data. The extensions come with identifiability guarantees, addressing whether the model can be distinguished from alternatives using the information it represents. The authors also develop methods for estimating these models by matching statistical moments.

The estimation approach connects the new models to discrete independent component analysis. This connection allows cumulant tensors to be extended to a discrete version of canonical correlation analysis. A further link to independent component analysis leads to generalized covariance matrices that can replace those tensors. The authors report that this substitution improves sample complexity and substantially simplifies both the derivations and the algorithms.

Standard tensor power methods and orthogonal joint diagonalization do not apply in this setting, so the paper uses non-orthogonal joint diagonalization to match cumulants. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the proposed models and estimation procedures. The contribution combines identifiable modeling extensions with a more manageable route to estimating them.
icml-2016-beyond-cca-moment-matching-for.tldr: Three identifiable extensions of probabilistic CCA use moment matching and generalized covariance matrices to simplify estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover communities when available evidence mostly connects nearby nodes. Each measurement gives a noisy indication of whether a pair belongs to the same community or to different communities. The motivating settings include social networks and computational biology, where the pattern of available comparisons can be strongly local.

The key modeling change concerns which node pairs are measured. Many existing models assume comparisons are sampled uniformly across all pairs. Here, measurements come mainly or entirely from nearby nodes. Consequently, the recovery problem must be solved using a locally concentrated pattern of evidence, making locality central to the analysis and algorithm design.

The authors present two algorithms whose running times are nearly linear in the number of measurements. Both achieve the information limits for exact recovery in the setting studied. This combines computational efficiency with recovery guarantees that reach the limits imposed by the available information. The result shows that local measurement structure can be accommodated while retaining both properties.
icml-2016-community-recovery-in-graphs-w.tldr: Two nearly linear-time algorithms achieve information limits for exact community recovery from noisy local measurements.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation asks how well a new decision policy would perform using data generated by a different policy. This is valuable when evaluating a candidate policy is a prerequisite to adopting it. The paper addresses a central difficulty: existing general approaches can introduce uncontrolled bias or produce estimates with high variance.

The authors extend a doubly robust estimator from bandit problems to sequential decision making. The resulting estimator is guaranteed to be unbiased and can have substantially lower variance than importance sampling estimators. The distinction matters: unbiasedness concerns systematic error, while reduced variance means estimates can fluctuate less across collected datasets. The variance improvement is presented as a possibility, rather than a universal outcome.

Experiments demonstrate accuracy on several benchmark problems and show how the estimator can serve within safe policy improvement. The paper also studies fundamental limits on evaluation accuracy. In certain scenarios, the estimator matches the theoretical lower bound, connecting its practical use with a qualified optimality result about how well the problem can be solved.
icml-2016-doubly-robust-off-policy-value.tldr: A sequential doubly robust estimator provides unbiased off-policy evaluation with potentially much lower variance than importance sampling.

paragraphs: Random projections reduce data dimensionality and can make learning computationally cheaper. This paper asks whether accurate, differentially private empirical risk minimization remains possible when the learner has access only to projected data and the projection matrix. The question combines two requirements: learning from compressed inputs and protecting privacy.

For generalized linear functions, the authors establish excess-risk bounds in this compressed setting. Writing n for the sample size and w(Theta) for the Gaussian width of the parameter space, the stated bounds scale as O(w(Theta)^(2/3)/n^(1/3)) under epsilon-differential privacy and O((w(Theta)/n)^(1/2)) under approximate differential privacy. These expressions connect the guarantees to sample size and the geometry of the parameter space.

The results answer the compressed-learning question affirmatively for the specified function class. They also have a consequence for learning with access to the original data: for a large class of empirical risk minimization problems, the analysis improves previously established worst-case risk bounds under epsilon-differential privacy. The contribution is theoretical, linking compression, privacy, and statistical accuracy.
icml-2016-efficient-private-empirical-ri.tldr: Private learning from random projections admits excess-risk guarantees for generalized linear functions, with bounds governed by parameter-space geometry.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately labels can be recovered by combining judgments from amateur workers. It works under the Dawid-Skene probabilistic model and focuses on the optimal aggregation error. The goal is a precise characterization of how the number of workers and their collective ability determine achievable accuracy.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds with error exponent mI(pi). Here, m counts workers, and I(pi) is their average Chernoff information, which summarizes collective labeling ability. Matching bounds identify the same exponent from both achievable performance and fundamental impossibility arguments. This makes the result more precise than a broad statement that additional workers reduce error.

The characterization yields the stated worker requirement m ≥ log(1/epsilon)/I(pi) for achieving epsilon misclassification error. It also implies optimality for various expectation-maximization algorithms when they begin with accurate estimates of the model parameters. That initialization condition is essential to the stated algorithmic conclusion. Together, the results relate workforce quality, workforce size, and the performance of practical aggregation procedures.
icml-2016-exact-exponent-in-optimal-rate.tldr: Matching error bounds precisely connect crowdsourcing accuracy to worker count and collective ability, with conditional optimality for EM algorithms.

paragraphs: Experimental design concerns choosing informative experiments when resources are limited. This paper examines that problem for sparse linear models, which are common in high-dimensional learning and statistics. Although optimal design has a substantial statistical literature, the authors identify a shortage of efficient strategies tailored to this sparse modeling setting.

The main formulation uses a linear regression function with an l1 regularizer. The paper proposes two design strategies, one motivated by geometry and another by algebra. Both lead to tractable algorithms, and the methods also apply to a more general class of sparse linear models. Their purpose is to make budget-constrained design computationally manageable within these modeling frameworks.

Experiments on benchmarks and a large neuroscience study spanning multiple sites show practical effectiveness. The neuroscience application suggests that the ideas may make a modest contribution to enrollment strategies for similar studies. That prospective use is qualified: the reported application supports possible relevance to study planning, while the central contribution remains the two efficient experimental-design approaches for sparse regression.
icml-2016-experimental-design-on-a-budge.tldr: Two tractable experimental-design strategies support budget-constrained sparse regression and show practical promise in benchmark and neuroscience studies.

paragraphs: Finding the nearest data points becomes difficult in high-dimensional spaces. This paper argues that part of this difficulty comes from partitioning space, the strategy underlying many search methods. It introduces a randomized alternative that avoids dividing the vector space into regions and supports retrieval of k nearest neighbors.

The algorithm has stated running-time dependence that is linear in ambient dimensionality and sublinear in both intrinsic dimensionality and dataset size. Its space usage is independent of ambient dimensionality and linear in dataset size. These properties address different aspects of scalability: the cost of answering a query and the storage needed by the search method.

The approach also allows accuracy and speed to be adjusted separately for each query, adapts automatically to changes in data density, and supports updates to the dataset. The authors provide theoretical properties and empirical comparisons against locality-sensitive hashing. In those comparisons, the method improves approximation quality, speed, and space efficiency, supporting its practical appeal alongside its stated computational guarantees.
icml-2016-fast-k-nearest-neighbour-searc.tldr: Dynamic Continuous Indexing avoids space partitioning and offers efficient, adjustable nearest-neighbor search with support for dataset updates.

paragraphs: Numerical rank concerns the effective non-null part of a matrix when small spectral components may reflect noise. This paper presents two inexpensive estimation techniques built from three computational ingredients. Both aim to count the relevant spectral directions through an approximate projection onto the corresponding invariant subspace.

First, a polynomial filter approximates that projection. The two proposed filter constructions use Hermite interpolation and Chebyshev expansions. Second, stochastic trace estimation approximates the trace of the projector, which gives the rank of the selected subspace. This turns rank estimation into a combination of filtering and randomized estimation of a matrix quantity.

The third ingredient determines where the filter should separate relevant eigenvalues from noise. The authors use spectral density and Lanczos spectroscopy to locate a gap between those groups. Detecting such a gap is necessary for obtaining a good filter in the proposed approach. The method therefore connects the rank estimate directly to a spectral separation that guides which directions should count.
icml-2016-fast-methods-for-estimating-th.tldr: Two rank-estimation methods combine polynomial filtering, stochastic trace estimation, and spectral-gap detection.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the convergence analysis of Online Proximal Gradient, Regularized Dual Averaging, and ADMM with online proximal gradient. Earlier results gave an O(log T/T) rate under strong convexity of the loss and an O(1/sqrt(T)) rate in the weakly convex case. The authors investigate whether the faster guarantee requires the stronger assumption.

Their result establishes the O(log T/T) rate when the expected loss is locally strongly convex. This relaxes both where the curvature condition must hold and which quantity must satisfy it. The condition applies to the expectation of the loss and is local, making it substantially weaker than the earlier strong-convexity requirement described in the abstract.

The authors identify Lasso and logistic regression among practical formulations satisfying the weaker condition. The result broadens the circumstances in which these existing algorithms have fast convergence guarantees. Its contribution is an improved analysis of established methods, together with a general approach that can guide sharper convergence analyses for stochastic and online optimization.
icml-2016-fast-rate-analysis-of-some-sto.tldr: Three stochastic optimization methods retain fast convergence guarantees when only the expected loss is locally strongly convex.

paragraphs: Softmax with cross-entropy is widely used to train convolutional classifiers, but the paper argues that it does not explicitly encourage discriminative feature structure. The authors introduce Large-Margin Softmax, or L-Softmax, to make that structure part of the training objective. The aim is to improve how learned features distinguish classes.

The loss encourages features from the same class to be compact and features from different classes to be separated. It also allows the desired margin to be adjusted. The authors state that the approach can avoid overfitting and show that it can be optimized with ordinary stochastic gradient descent, making the changed objective compatible with a standard training method.

Experiments on four benchmark datasets found that L-Softmax produced more discriminative deep features and significantly improved visual classification and verification performance. These results connect the intended feature geometry with observed task improvements. The paper's contribution is a supervision component that explicitly shapes within-class similarity and between-class separation, with empirical support across the evaluated visual tasks.
icml-2016-large-margin-softmax-loss-for-.tldr: L-Softmax explicitly encourages compact classes and stronger separation, improving visual classification and verification in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to build a global classifier when private training data remain with multiple parties. Each party contributes a locally trained classifier, while the global learning procedure has no access to the underlying private data. The challenge is to combine their knowledge accurately while providing differential privacy.

The proposed framework uses the local ensemble to create labeled training information from auxiliary unlabeled data. A global private classifier then learns from that information. The authors find majority voting too sensitive for this purpose, so they introduce a risk function weighted by class probabilities estimated from the ensemble. This changes how local predictions guide global training.

Relative to a non-private solution, the stated generalization-error bound scales as O(epsilon^-2 M^-2), where M is the number of participating parties. The result supports strong privacy without performance loss when participation is sufficiently large. Evaluations on activity recognition, network intrusion detection, and malicious URL detection demonstrate the framework across realistic tasks, linking the privacy analysis with practical classification settings.
icml-2016-learning-privately-from-multip.tldr: A private global classifier learns from local-model predictions on auxiliary data, with an error bound that improves as participation grows.

paragraphs: This paper improves block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe optimization, focusing on structured support vector machines. Its central observation is that estimated gaps for individual blocks reveal how suboptimal those blocks remain. These estimates can therefore guide adaptive decisions throughout optimization, giving the algorithm information about where work is most useful.

The authors use block gaps to sample training objects nonuniformly at each iteration. They also incorporate pairwise and away-step Frank-Wolfe variants into the block-coordinate framework. A further improvement caches oracle calls and uses a gap-based criterion to decide when a cached result is acceptable. Together, these changes apply the same suboptimality information to sampling, updates, and reuse of computation.

The paper additionally introduces what it identifies as the first method for computing an approximate regularization path for structured support vector machines. An extensive empirical evaluation covers all proposed methods on four structured-prediction datasets. The contribution is a coordinated set of optimization tools built around block-gap estimates, with applications extending beyond the principal structured-SVM setting.
icml-2016-minding-the-gaps-for-block-fra.tldr: Block-gap estimates guide adaptive sampling, update variants, caching, and regularization-path computation for structured-SVM optimization.

paragraphs: Network morphism changes a trained neural network's architecture while completely preserving the function it computes. This paper develops a systematic framework for doing so. Preserving the parent network's behavior allows the child network to inherit learned knowledge, with the potential for further growth and substantially shorter subsequent training.

The authors formulate network morphism equations and develop algorithms for changing depth, width, kernel size, and subnet structure. The methods cover both classic neural networks and convolutional networks. This breadth matters because architectural growth can take several forms, and a useful preservation scheme must accommodate more than a single type of modification.

Nonlinear activations create another requirement for function-preserving transformations. The paper introduces a family of parameterized activation functions to facilitate morphing neurons with any continuous nonlinear activation. Benchmark experiments on typical networks demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness. The exact preservation objective concerns the transformation itself; becoming a more powerful model through continued training is presented as the resulting network's potential.
icml-2016-network-morphism-5f71ddaea0.tldr: Network morphism changes trained network architectures while preserving their functions, enabling knowledge reuse during further growth.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Representation is used to separate data generated from a union of subspaces. Its computational burden includes working with a nuclear-norm-regularized matrix containing one row and column per sample. For n samples, that matrix has n squared entries, making memory consumption a substantial obstacle as the dataset grows.

This paper develops an online implementation that reduces memory cost from O(n^2) to O(pd). Here, p is the ambient dimension and d is an estimated rank, with d < p < n. The stated ordering makes the difference meaningful: storage depends on the ambient dimension and estimated rank instead of a matrix covering every pair of samples.

The authors prove that the generated solution sequence converges asymptotically to a stationary point of the expected loss. This is a stationary-point guarantee, rather than a claim of global optimality. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets further support the method's speed, robustness, and memory efficiency, connecting the storage improvement with practical evidence and an accompanying convergence result.
icml-2016-online-low-rank-subspace-clust.tldr: An online Low-Rank Representation method reduces memory to O(pd) and converges asymptotically to a stationary point.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of true task labels from noisy crowd judgments under the Dawid-Skene model. Existing algorithms had guarantees that remained noticeably above the fundamental error limit. The authors investigate whether belief propagation can close that gap and how its guarantees change with the number of tasks assigned to workers.

When each worker receives at most two tasks, they establish a tighter lower bound and prove that belief propagation matches it exactly. Within this scenario, no algorithm can correctly label a larger fraction of tasks according to the information-theoretic limit. The result is stronger than a comparison with a selected collection of competing methods.

For workers assigned more than two tasks, the paper establishes that belief propagation outperforms existing algorithms with known provable guarantees. Experiments suggest near-optimal behavior across all regimes considered, while other evaluated methods appear suboptimal. The distinctions matter: exact optimality is proved in the restricted assignment scenario, broader dominance is established theoretically, and broader near-optimality is supported empirically.
icml-2016-optimality-of-belief-propagati.tldr: Belief propagation is provably optimal when each crowd worker has at most two tasks, with broader theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes maximum-likelihood estimation for generalized Thurstone models, where an observation records a choice from a set of at least two items. The authors give tight descriptions of mean squared estimation error. They also establish necessary and sufficient conditions for correct classification when items belong to one of two classes.

The analysis examines how accuracy depends jointly on the choice model and the arrangement of comparison sets. For structures that are unbiased in advance, including independently and uniformly sampled sets, the observations needed for a target accuracy depend on the particular generalized Thurstone model. This makes model selection relevant to the statistical value of collected choices.

For a broad family containing the popular models used in practice, estimation error is largely insensitive to the number of items in each comparison set. However, other models exist for which error falls much faster as sets grow. The finding qualifies the intuition that larger comparison sets necessarily provide substantially better estimates: their benefit depends on the underlying choice model.
icml-2016-parameter-estimation-for-gener.tldr: Estimation guarantees show that the benefit of larger comparison sets depends strongly on the generalized Thurstone choice model.

paragraphs: This paper studies policies that imitate demonstrated behavior while responding to context arriving sequentially in a dynamic, continuous environment. The goal includes smooth behavior, so learning must account for how responses evolve over time. A complex relationship between context and behavior makes this more demanding than simply matching isolated demonstrated outputs.

The authors reduce the imitation-learning problem to regression. This allows complex function classes to represent the context-to-behavior mapping, while regularization enforces smoothness. They then introduce a learning meta-algorithm designed to reach a good policy quickly and stably. The reduction connects the behavioral objective to a regression problem that explicitly includes the desired smoothness property.

The approach is fully deterministic and uses an adaptive learning rate. The authors prove that this rate can yield larger policy improvements than previous approaches, and the method can ensure stable convergence. Empirical results show significant performance gains over earlier methods. Together, the contributions address expressive behavior modeling, controlled changes in behavior, and stability of the learning process.
icml-2016-smooth-imitation-learning-for-.tldr: Smooth imitation learning is reduced to regularized regression, with a deterministic adaptive procedure supporting stable policy improvement.

paragraphs: Learning-based controllers can be appealing alternatives to controllers derived through classical control theory, but missing performance guarantees can prevent practical adoption. This paper develops a stability-analysis tool for controllers whose system dynamics are represented by Gaussian processes. It considers arbitrary Markovian control policies and separates two ways of using the learned dynamics.

In the first setting, the dynamics are represented by the Gaussian process mean. The tool identifies a region of state space in which the closed-loop system is provably stable. This gives a regional guarantee: the analysis establishes where stability holds for the combined controller and modeled system.

In the second setting, the analysis uses the full Gaussian process distribution. The abstract states that infinite-horizon stability guarantees cannot exist in this case, so the tool instead studies stability over a finite time interval. Simulated benchmark evaluations support the theoretical results. The contribution is therefore sensitive to how uncertainty enters the dynamics, providing different forms of stability analysis for the two representations.
icml-2016-stability-of-controllers-for-g.tldr: A stability tool provides regional guarantees for GP-mean dynamics and finite-time analysis for full GP dynamics.

paragraphs: Stochastic-gradient Monte Carlo methods make sampling more scalable, but can mix poorly when variables are strongly coupled or have very different scales. This paper introduces a method that adapts sampling to local geometry using ideas from quasi-Newton optimization. The goal is to improve movement through the target distribution without expensive geometric calculations.

The method approximates the inverse Hessian using a limited history of samples and gradients. It uses dense approximations, allowing it to account for interactions between variables, while keeping time and memory costs linear in the problem dimension. This combination addresses the computational difficulty of incorporating richer geometry into large-scale sampling.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing asymptotic unbiasedness and consistency for posterior expectations. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate effectiveness. On two challenging applications, convergence was comparable to Riemannian approaches, while computational requirements were similar to diagonal preconditioning methods. These comparisons support the intended balance between informative geometric adaptation and low computational cost in the evaluated settings.
icml-2016-stochastic-quasi-newton-langev.tldr: Quasi-Newton geometry improves stochastic-gradient sampling while retaining linear time and memory costs and asymptotic estimation guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper treats text classification as jointly learning a linear classifier and a nonlinear feature generator. The feature generator embeds regions of text and then pools their representations. Within this framework, the authors investigate LSTMs as a way to represent regions whose lengths can vary and may be large.

The variable-length capability distinguishes the proposed LSTM region embeddings from the fixed region sizes used in convolutional networks. The work explores effective and efficient use in both supervised and semi-supervised learning. Its best results combine LSTM-based and convolution-based region embeddings trained on unlabeled data, bringing the two forms of representation together.

The reported performance exceeds previous best results on four benchmark datasets. The findings indicate that, for this classification task, embeddings of text regions are more useful than embeddings of individual words considered separately. Regions can convey complex concepts, making the unit of representation central to the paper's argument. The empirical conclusion concerns the evaluated text-categorization setting and supports learning features over larger stretches of text.
icml-2016-supervised-and-semi-supervised.tldr: Combining LSTM and convolutional text-region embeddings learned from unlabeled data improved classification across four benchmarks.

paragraphs: Clustering depends on both how data are represented and how groups are formed from that representation. This paper observes that much research has focused on distance measures and grouping algorithms, with less attention to learning representations specifically for clustering. It introduces Deep Embedded Clustering, or DEC, to address that part of the problem.

DEC uses a deep neural network to map data into a lower-dimensional feature space. Within that space, it iteratively optimizes a clustering objective while learning both the representation and cluster assignments. This couples the features used to compare examples with the grouping task itself, making representation learning an integral part of clustering.

Evaluations on image and text corpora show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support the value of jointly learning the feature space and the groups, across the two evaluated types of data. The paper's central contribution is the combined learning procedure: it makes the representation responsive to the clustering objective throughout iterative optimization.
icml-2016-unsupervised-deep-embedding-fo.tldr: DEC jointly learns a lower-dimensional representation and cluster assignments, improving clustering on evaluated image and text datasets.
